strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored practical problem: prediction mismatch due to LLM non-determinism can catastrophically break arithmetic-coding-based model-driven compression, and framing this as a 'probability matching' problem is a useful contribution.

The PMATIC algorithm is clean, model-agnostic, and plausibly a drop-in replacement for arithmetic coding; the helper-bit design (quantize to bin center or boundary, communicate choice with low-entropy bits) is elegant and well motivated.

The theory is self-contained and correct: Proposition 1 (tanh bound on conditional TV from logit L∞ mismatch), Theorem 1 (correctness under dCTV ≤ δ), and the loss analysis giving an O(sqrt(δ log(1/δ))) tradeoff are clearly stated and proven.

Experiments demonstrate end-to-end correct decoding under injected mismatch on two text corpora, with a clear table showing overhead as a function of the tolerated mismatch bound, and strong absolute compression rates versus gzip.
Honest reporting of limitations (synthetic mismatch only, rolling context window, quantized model) and a transparent appendix on LLM usage in the work.
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow: the only external baseline is gzip, which is far from the state of the art for text compression (e.g., cmix, PAQ variants, zstd, nncp, or other LLM-based tools like LLMZip/llama-zip under the same setup). Claims of 'out-performing standard modern compression tools' are supported only against gzip.

Mismatch is only synthetic (IID uniform logit noise). The motivating phenomenon is real hardware/software-induced non-determinism; no experiment uses actual cross-hardware or cross-framework mismatch, so practical applicability remains unvalidated (acknowledged, but it weakens the central claim).

Missing related work on robust/mismatch-tolerant arithmetic coding, e.g., distributed arithmetic coding and error-resilient arithmetic decoding (Zou & Bloom, Grangetto et al.), and on the common alternative of transmitting quantized logits from encoder to decoder. There is no comparison to any competing mismatch-tolerance strategy, so it is unclear PMATIC's overhead is favorable; the claim of being the first to address prediction mismatch needs qualification.

The overhead is substantial at larger mismatch levels: ~2 bits/token over the no-mismatch baseline in Setting 1 (5.34 vs 2.81 on the 1000-article set), which sits uneasily with the 'without significant loss' phrasing; the results text also quotes the ≈0.2 bits/token figure that only matches the enwik8 setting, not the 1000-article setting (0.71).

The algorithm is conceptually simple (probability quantization plus side information), and the analysis is elementary; the contribution may be viewed as incremental relative to the robust coding and arithmetic-coding literature.
No runtime/throughput measurements despite helper bits roughly doubling the number of arithmetic-coded symbols per token, and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Practical scope questions are unaddressed: the mismatch bound must be known in advance to set δ and r, and model parameters (gigabytes) are excluded from reported file sizes; both deserve more careful treatment for the practicality claims.

strengths: Identifies a real and practically relevant problem: prediction mismatch due to LLM non-determinism genuinely breaks arithmetic coding in model-driven compression, and this is underexplored in the literature.

The PMATIC algorithm is simple, clean, and correct; the correctness proof (Theorem 1) is sound and the construction is a plausible drop-in replacement for arithmetic coding in existing LLM compression tools.
The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1, compression loss bounds, and the r-balancing argument in Eq. 21) is coherent and the empirical results are consistent with the theory.
The paper is clearly written, well-organized, and honestly discloses limitations (synthetic mismatch only) and LLM usage in an appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea is essentially probability quantization with flag ('helper') bits to resolve bin ambiguity. This is a fairly straightforward engineering fix, and the connection to prior robust/quantized coding techniques is not seriously examined; the claim of being 'the first work to explicitly address' prediction mismatch feels overstated given the long history of robust arithmetic coding under adaptive-model mismatch.

Weak baselines: the only comparison is against gzip, a decades-old and easily beaten strawman for LLM-based compression. No comparison to zstd/xz/bzip2/cmix/NNCP/ts_zip, and crucially no comparison against any alternative mismatch-tolerant coding scheme (e.g., naive probability quantization without helper bits, or coder-side deterministic fallbacks), so the contribution of PMATIC itself is never isolated.

The motivating use case is never actually tested: all mismatch is synthetically injected IID uniform noise on logits. No experiment reproduces real GPU/library non-determinism across hardware, software versions, or computation orders, so the paper's central practical claim ('robust to real LLM non-determinism') is not validated.

Evaluation is thin: only two text datasets, two (r, δ) settings, a fixed random 17-bit token mapping (an avoidable per-token overhead), a truncated rolling context window, and a single quantized 8B model. No ablations on bin choice, alphabet mapping, or context length, and no variance analysis over runs.

The compression-loss analysis relies on a strong uniformity-within-bin assumption and yields only loose asymptotic bounds; no lower bounds or discussion of how far PMATIC is from optimal under the mismatch model.
No code release or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and the experimental setup (quantized Llama 3.1, specific quantization scheme) is underspecified for exact reproduction.

Significance is limited by the paper's own admission (Section 6): without validation under real-world mismatch, and without evidence over stronger baselines, PMATIC remains a proof of concept rather than a demonstrated advance.

strengths: Identifies a genuine, previously under-addressed practical problem: LLM non-determinism breaks arithmetic coding in model-driven compression, and formalizes it cleanly (mismatch-tolerant coding, dCTV, bounded logit mismatch).

The PMATIC algorithm is simple, model-agnostic, and elegant: probability quantization into bins plus low-entropy 'helper' bits, framed as a drop-in replacement for the arithmetic coder in existing model-driven compressors.

Solid theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 (bounding dCTV by logit L∞ mismatch), Theorem 1 (correctness proof under bounded conditional TV distance), and a loss analysis that yields an interpretable choice of bin radius r with total overhead O(sqrt(delta log(1/delta))). The theory–experiment agreement is convincing (predicted r ≈ 0.047 vs. chosen 0.05).

Experiments validate the correctness claim end-to-end (all files decoded successfully under injected mismatch) and quantify the robustness/overhead tradeoff across two robustness levels, showing graceful degradation relative to the no-mismatch upper bound.
Clear writing overall; the problem statement, algorithm description (Sections 3.1–3.2), and analysis are easy to follow, and the paper is transparent about LLM usage in an appendix.
weaknesses: Mismatch is only synthetic: decoder noise is injected as IID uniform logit perturbations. Real GPU/library non-determinism may not be IID, may be correlated across tokens/layers, and its magnitude is not measured — the central practical claim (robustness to real LLM non-determinism) is not directly validated.

Weak baselines and an overstated comparison: the only external baseline is gzip, which is not a 'modern standard' for text compression (xz/zstd/brotli are substantially better, and learned compressors like cmix/NNCP/ts_zip are far stronger on enwik8). The claim that PMATIC 'out-performs standard modern compression tools' is not supported by the evidence presented.

The fixed-length 17-bit token encoding is a notable inefficiency: the method cannot exploit the token distribution itself, inflating bits-per-token relative to token-ID arithmetic coding; the practical significance of the reported rates is hard to judge without this being ablated or justified.

Considerable robustness overhead: roughly 2 bits/token (~0.4 bits per 17-bit token code) at epsilon = 0.002, which is a large cost relative to entropy; the paper does not explore cheaper alternatives (e.g., error-correcting-code or resynchronization-style approaches) or compare against them.

Scope is narrow: text-only, a single quantized 8B model, small rolling context (512), small file sizes, no runtime/computation cost measurements, and no code release mentioned, limiting reproducibility and significance.

The compression-loss analysis rests on simplifying assumptions (uniformity of encoder probabilities within bins, encoder probabilities equal true probabilities); the footnote workaround (PRNG bin translation) is mentioned but not analyzed or tested.

Positioning on novelty could be tightened: robust/quantized coding and mismatch-tolerant source coding ideas exist in the information theory literature (e.g., mismatched coding, error-resilient arithmetic coding), and the paper's 'first work' claim needs more careful delineation.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a real, practically important problem (prediction mismatch from non-determinism in LLM-driven lossless compression) that has been largely unaddressed, with a clear problem statement and a natural mismatch-tolerance definition (Section 2).

PMATIC is a clean, model-agnostic, drop-in replacement for arithmetic coding; the helper-bit/bin-quantization mechanism is simple and well-explained (with a helpful worked example in A.2 and Figure 2).

Theoretical contributions are sound and complete: Proposition 1 connects L∞ logit bounds to conditional TV distance (with a full appendix proof), Theorem 1 proves decoding correctness under bounded mismatch, and Section 4.2 derives a sensible O(√(δ log(1/δ))) overhead bound with an approximately optimal choice of r.

Experiments cover three LLMs, several datasets (including non-English text), and multiple robustness settings; Table 1 shows PMATIC still substantially outperforms cmix/brotli/xz/gzip/zstd even at the most robust setting tested, so the robustness overhead does not destroy the practical advantage of model-driven compression.

Validation goes beyond synthetic noise: a real two-machine experiment (Apple M2 Pro vs. M4 Max) demonstrates cascading failure of standard arithmetic coding and successful decoding with δ=0.01, giving a credible proof of concept; the paper is honest about limitations (stochastic rather than strict bounds, uniformity assumption being inaccurate per Table 2).
Transparent disclosure of LLM usage (A.5) and clear overall writing.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea—quantizing predicted probabilities into bins and communicating agreement via low-entropy side information—is a fairly direct modification of arithmetic coding, and concurrent work (Hu & Tang, 2026) addresses a closely related problem with a similar construction ('longform' terminology shared). No comparison to that approach is provided.

The strict bounded-mismatch assumption is the weakest link in practice: the authors' own appendix suggests real non-determinism is stochastic and only approximately bounded; setting δ=0.001 (moderate overhead) failed on all real-machine files, meaning the practical setting requires δ=0.01, where overhead is large (e.g., enwik8 compression ratio 0.078 → 0.249 for LLaMA 3.1).

Real non-determinism experiments are small in scale (150 files of 5 KB, a single model, two Apple laptops) and rely on a rough empirical estimate of the logit-discrepancy bound from a single 810-token prompt; the guarantee of correctness on other hardware/model pairs is not established.

Known inefficiencies are left unaddressed: helper bits are encoded with the uniformity-assumption probability δ/r even though Table 2 shows the true fraction is far lower, and the fixed-length 'longform' token encoding ignores token probabilities; the paper acknowledges both could yield significant improvement but does not implement them.

The compression-loss analysis rests on simplifying assumptions (true model probabilities, uniform bin occupancy) that the authors' own data contradict, so the O(√(δ log(1/δ))) bound may not tightly characterize actual overhead.
Scope is narrow: only text compression is evaluated; claims of generality to other domains (images, etc.) are deferred to future work.
No release of code or longform dictionaries is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the quantitative results.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a real and underexplored problem — prediction mismatch between encoder and decoder LLMs in model-driven lossless compression — which is practically relevant given documented non-determinism in GPU inference.

PMATIC is a simple, model-agnostic, drop-in construction (probability quantization plus cheap helper bits) with a clean correctness proof (Theorem 1) and a reasonable overhead analysis yielding an O(sqrt(δ log(1/δ))) loss bound and a principled choice of bin width (Eq. 20).

The experimental design sensibly isolates the robustness overhead by comparing PMATIC against standard arithmetic coding within otherwise-identical pipelines, and Table 2 honestly exposes that the uniformity assumption underlying the loss analysis is conservative in practice.

Both synthetic (bounded logit noise) and real (cross-device, two different Apple SoCs) non-determinism are tested, and the appendix provides useful implementation details and illustrative decoding-failure examples.
The paper is clearly written, with a helpful worked encoding example (A.2) and transparent disclosure of LLM assistance in A.5.
weaknesses: The practical significance of the results is questionable: the robustness setting that actually worked under real non-determinism (δ=0.01) roughly triples the compressed size relative to no-PMATIC (e.g., 0.0780 → 0.2492 on enwik8 for LLaMA 3.1), eroding much of the advantage of LLM-based compression. The paper does not confront this tradeoff directly.

The real non-determinism evaluation is very small: only two machines (both Apple laptops), 100 Wikipedia articles plus 250 KB of Emma, and a single model. The claim that δ=0.01 bounds cross-device logit discrepancy is supported by one histogram on one prompt (Fig. 3) and is unlikely to generalize across GPU vendors, quantization settings, or software stacks; the correctness guarantee could silently fail out-of-distribution.

The synthetic-noise experiment only injects noise that provably satisfies the theoretical bound, so it largely confirms the trivial direction of Theorem 1 rather than stress-testing the mismatch model; there is no experiment probing behavior at or just beyond the bound.

Only text compression is evaluated, and the fixed-length 'longform' dictionary (random ℓ-bit assignment per token) discards token-frequency structure, adding avoidable overhead that conflates with PMATIC's robustness cost; no ablation of the longform design is given.

No quantitative comparison with the closely related concurrent work (Hu & Tang, 2026) or with mismatch-mitigation alternatives (e.g., deterministic backends) despite both being discussed; the positioning is limited to citation.

The compression-loss analysis (Section 4.2) rests on a strong 'worst-case non-adversarial' uniformity assumption that the paper's own Table 2 shows is off by an order of magnitude, and the resulting 2x-optimality argument is heuristic; the fundamental limits of the problem are left open, which limits the theoretical contribution's depth.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility of the LLM-pipeline experiments.

strengths: Identifies and formally defines an important, underexplored practical problem (prediction mismatch / non-determinism in LLM-driven lossless compression) and provides a clean problem statement and mismatch-tolerance framework (Section 2).

Proposes PMATIC, a simple, model-agnostic, drop-in replacement for arithmetic coding with a full correctness proof (Theorem 1) connecting logit-level L∞ bounds to conditional TV distance (Proposition 1), plus a theoretical overhead analysis yielding an O(sqrt(δ log(1/δ))) bound and a principled bin-radius choice (Eq. 20).

Experiments span multiple LLMs (LLaMA 3.1, Mistral, Qwen 2.5), multiple datasets including non-English text, and both synthetic noise and real cross-device non-determinism tests, with sensible baselines (standard arithmetic coding within identical pipelines, plus gzip/xz/brotli/bzip2/zstd/cmix).

Honest and thorough analysis of its own assumptions: Table 2 empirically validates the uniformity assumption on helper bits and quantifies the headroom left from suboptimal helper-bit coding; limitations and future work are candidly discussed (e.g., stochastic vs. bounded mismatch).
Clear, reproducible write-up including implementation details, a worked encoding example (Appendix A.2), and an explicit LLM-usage disclosure (A.5).
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation is limited in scale and scope: the real non-determinism test uses only two Apple laptops, 100 Wikipedia articles plus 250 KB of Emma, and only one model family; broader hardware/software diversity would substantially strengthen the practical claims.

The robustness level required in practice (δ = 0.01) incurs a large overhead (e.g., 0.078 → 0.249 compression ratio on enwik8), so the operating point that actually works across machines is notably less efficient; the paper does not deeply analyze how to close this gap beyond noting helper-bit probability improvements as future work.

No empirical comparison with the closely related concurrent work (Hu & Tang 2026), the only other mismatch-tolerant coding approach cited; a head-to-head comparison or at least a theoretical comparison of overhead would significantly strengthen positioning.

The compression-loss analysis rests on simplifying assumptions (encoder predictions are 'true' probabilities; uniform distribution within bins) that are only partially validated, and the optimality claim ('at most 2x optimal') is approximate rather than rigorous.
Evaluation is limited to text compression; claims of being a general drop-in replacement are not tested on other modalities (e.g., images), where mismatch characteristics may differ.

Only categorical guarantees under bounded mismatch are provided; the practically relevant stochastic-mismatch regime (where real non-determinism evidently lives) is left to future work, and the δ chosen empirically (0.01) is only 'a reasonable estimate' of the true bound, so correctness in practice is not fully guaranteed by the theory.
